extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners reviewing MPEP guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining whether patent claims satisfy 35 U.S.C. §101 (statutory categories and exclusion of judicial exceptions) using the Alice/Mayo two‑part framework, claim construction (BRI), and related procedural practices for examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory categories requirement (Step 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: First, the claimed invention must be to one of the four statutory categories: processes, machines, manufactures and compositions of matter (35 U.S.C. 101).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines ‘process’ (actions or series of acts) and explains that machines, manufactures, and compositions are physical/tangible 'things.' For product claims (machines/manufactures/compositions) the claimed subject matter must exist in some physical or tangible form. Non-limiting examples of claims not falling in the categories include information/data per se, computer program per se (software per se), transitory signals/carrier waves, and subject matter excluded by statute (e.g., humans per se under AIA). If the BRI of a claim covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments, the claim fails Step 1; examiners should point out the BRI and recommend narrowing amendments when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial exceptions exclusion / Alice‑Mayo two‑part framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Second, the claimed invention must not be directed to a judicial exception (abstract ideas, laws of nature, natural phenomena) unless the claim as a whole includes additional limitations amounting to significantly more than the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The MPEP adopts the Alice/Mayo two-part test: (1) determine whether claims are directed to an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon (Step 2A); (2) if so, determine whether the claim recites additional elements that amount to significantly more (Step 2B) — the 'search for an inventive concept.' The Alice/Mayo test is the only test to use for §101. The machine‑or‑transformation test is a helpful clue, not a separate test. Do not evaluate eligibility by 'useful, concrete, and tangible result' or by utility; do not treat mere recitation of concrete components or field‑of‑use as dispositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) before eligibility analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Before examining a claim for eligibility, the examiner must establish the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BRI sets the boundaries of coverage sought and influences whether a claim covers non-statutory subject matter or a judicial exception. Claim construction affects Step 1 and both parts of the Alice/Mayo test. Examples (Mentor Graphics, Synopsys, Enfish, Amdocs) show how different constructions can change eligibility findings. When BRI covers non‑statutory embodiments, reject and recommend amendment to narrow scope. See MPEP §2111 for BRI details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility Step 1 procedural determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 1 asks: Is the claim to a process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter (after BRI and review of disclosure)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claim as a whole does not fall within any statutory category (Step 1: NO) reject under 35 U.S.C. 101 (use form paragraphs 7.05/7.05.01). If claim falls within one or more categories (Step 1: YES), proceed to Step 2A to determine whether it is directed to a judicial exception. If amendment could make claim statutory, examiner should recommend amendment and may proceed to Pathways A/B/C analysis for eligibility of the amended claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A — Whether claim is directed to a judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims directed to nothing more than abstract ideas, natural phenomena, or laws of nature are not eligible. The examiner should identify the particular exception implicated and analyze whether the claim is 'directed to' that exception (considering claim limitations and BRI). See MPEP §2106.04 and cited case law (Diehr, Alice, Mayo, Benson, Flook, Chakrabarty, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract idea groupings and tentative abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify and identify abstract ideas by recognized groupings and identify tentative abstract ideas when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP provides example lists and groupings of abstract ideas and notes that some concepts may be tentatively considered abstract pending analysis. Examiners should use these groupings and examples to help identify whether a claim recites an abstract idea, but apply full Alice/Mayo analysis rather than rely solely on grouping labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of a judicial exception into a practical application (Step 2A prong two)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim integrates the judicial exception into a practical application such that it is not 'directed to' the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integration into a practical application can make a claim eligible at Step 2A (prong two) by showing the exception is applied in a specific way tied to a practical implementation. Consider whether claim limitations impose meaningful practical limits (e.g., particular machines, improvements in computer or other technology, particular treatment). Case law (Diehr, Enfish, McRO) provides examples where integration or improvement led to eligibility. See MPEP §2106.04(d) and §2106.04(d)(1)/(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different characteristics analysis (products of nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: For claims involving natural products, analyze whether the claimed subject matter has markedly different characteristics from the naturally occurring counterpart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimed product exhibits markedly different characteristics (structure, function, or other properties) from what exists in nature, it may not be a judicial exception and may be eligible. Use the 'markedly different characteristics' test and applicable case law (e.g., Myriad) to assess whether a claimed composition or organism is a product of nature or a patent‑eligible human-made invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B — Whether claim recites additional elements amounting to 'significantly more' (inventive concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: If claim is directed to a judicial exception, determine whether additional claim elements, individually or in combination, transform the nature of the claim into a patent‑eligible application (i.e., whether they amount to significantly more than the exception).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'significantly more' inquiry looks for an inventive concept beyond the judicial exception. MPEP §2106.05 enumerates categories of considerations (improvements to technology, particular machine, particular transformation, whether elements are conventional/routine, other meaningful limitations, etc.) to determine if 'significantly more' exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements to the functioning of a computer or to any other technology (as evidence of 'significantly more')
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed improvement to the functioning of a computer or other technology or technical field can constitute 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim provides a technical improvement or an unconventional solution to a technological problem (e.g., improving database performance or computer operation), that improvement can show the claim amounts to significantly more than an abstract idea. Refer to Enfish, McRO, and related MPEP guidance (§2106.04(d)(1) and §2106.05(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular machine limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Recitation of a particular machine in the claims can support eligibility if the machine is specific and confines the claim beyond a generic computer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims tied to a particular machine may limit the claim's scope sufficiently to amount to significantly more; however, merely reciting a generic computer or 'special purpose' computer is often insufficient. Evaluate whether the machine is particular and plays a meaningful role in implementing the claimed invention (§2106.05(b)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular transformation (machine‑or‑transformation consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed transformation of a particular article to a different state or thing can support eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The machine‑or‑transformation test is a useful clue to eligibility: a particular transformation of an article can indicate that the claim poses patent‑eligible subject matter. But do not treat M‑O‑T as a separate test; consider it within the Alice/Mayo framework (see §2106.05(c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Well‑understood, routine, conventional activity does not confer eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: If the additional elements beyond the judicial exception are well‑understood, routine, or conventional in the field, they do not amount to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must assess whether claimed additional elements merely recite conventional activity known in the art — if so, they cannot supply the inventive concept required at Step 2B (§2106.05(d)). Case law and MPEP examples illustrate when conventional features fail to transform an abstract idea into a patent‑eligible invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other meaningful limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations other than those specifically listed (machine, transformation, improvement) that meaningfully limit the exception may support eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims may include other types of meaningful limitations that, in context, render the claim significantly more than the judicial exception (e.g., specific ordered combinations of steps conferring technical effect). Evaluate whether such limitations add meaningful restrictions and practical application (§2106.05(e)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere instructions to apply an exception are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Claiming only instructions to apply a judicial exception (e.g., 'apply the algorithm') does not render the claim patent‑eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If additional claim language simply tells a practitioner to implement an abstract idea or law of nature without more (no technical implementation or meaningful limitations), it is not 'significantly more' (§2106.05(f)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant extra‑solution activity is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Activities that amount to insignificant extra‑solution activity (conventional data gathering, post‑solution activity) do not make a claim eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extra-solution activities that are token or insignificant — e.g., insignificant post‑solution steps, mere data gathering that does not meaningfully change the analysis — cannot supply the inventive concept (§2106.05(g)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Field of use or technological environment limitations alone are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Limiting the claim to a particular field of use or technological environment, by itself, does not make an otherwise abstract claim eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim cannot be rendered nonabstract merely by reciting that it is implemented on the Internet or in a particular field; need meaningful technical improvement or other significantly more features (§2106.05(h)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined analysis and eligibility pathways (Pathways A, B, C)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the flowchart pathways to determine eligibility: Pathway A (streamlined/self‑evident eligibility), Pathway B (falls within statutory category and not directed to judicial exception), Pathway C (directed to exception but recites significantly more).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If eligibility is self‑evident, examiners may use a streamlined Pathway A analysis (§2106.06). Pathway B applies when Step 1 = YES and Step 2A = NO (no exception). Pathway C applies when Step 1 = YES, Step 2A = YES, and Step 2B = YES (significantly more). If uncertain about streamlined analysis, perform full Alice/Mayo analysis. Claims not eligible under any pathway should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete examination — use of other statutory provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Regardless of a §101 rejection or eligibility finding, the examiner should complete examination of each claim under other patentability requirements (35 U.S.C. 102, 103, 112, utility, inventorship, and non‑statutory double patenting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §101 is a threshold inquiry but not the sole tool for patentability determinations; novelty, nonobviousness, and specification requirements may be applied to address deficiencies that §101 does not resolve (see Bilski and related citations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulating and supporting §101 rejections and evaluating applicant responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Use established form paragraphs and procedural practices when making §101 rejections and when evaluating applicant responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP provides guidance on formulating and supporting rejections for lack of subject matter eligibility, recommended form paragraphs (e.g., 7.05, 7.05.01), how to evaluate applicant arguments/evidence, and how to clarify the record (§2106.07). Examiners should explain reasons for the rejection, identify the judicial exception, provide claim analysis under Alice/Mayo, and note recommended claim amendments when appropriate.
